model.label: Tax-funded unified national health system (SUS), free at the point of use and run jointly by federal, state and municipal governments, alongside voluntary private health plans

overview.statement: Brazil's 1988 Constitution made health a universal right and a duty of the state; the unified health system (Sistema Único de Saúde, SUS), created in 1990, is the vehicle for progress towards universal coverage.
Two 1990 laws, 8.080 and 8.142, put the constitutional principle of health as a right into practice and defined how the system is organised.

From its start the SUS was meant to be universal, comprehensive and decentralised, and free of charge where services are delivered, resting on principles of equity, solidarity and social participation.

locator.section: Expansion of the Unified Health System in Brazil

overview.statement: Management of the system moved from a centralised social-security bureaucracy to shared (tripartite) governance by municipalities, states and the federal government.

Most basic health units (85%) are owned by municipalities, but the 2024 census of these units found 20% run under private management arrangements, with social health organisations, public-interest civil society organisations and charities taking a growing role, especially in large cities.

financing.statement: Minimum levels of health spending for each level of government (federal, state and municipal) were introduced in 2000 and written into law in 2012.

locator.section: Expansion of the Unified Health System in Brazil

financing.statement: Between 2003 and 2016 the federal government's share of public health spending fell from 50.0% to 40.8%.
States' share of public health spending rose from 22.3% in 2003 to 27.0% in 2016, and municipalities' share from 25.5% to 32.2%.

A 2018 analysis put public spending at 46.0% of Brazil's health spending, one of the lowest shares in Latin America and the Caribbean (average 51.28%), among upper-middle-income countries (55.2%) and among OECD countries (62.2%).

The Constitution makes the private sector complementary to the public one, but in practice the government partly subsidises it through tax breaks for people with private insurance, who also obtain high-complexity procedures in the SUS because their plans cover them poorly or reimburse little.
The SUS is financed from taxes collected by all three levels of government: the federal government, the states and the municipalities.

Since Constitutional Amendment 86 of 2015, the Constitution itself (art. 198, §2, I) sets the federal government's minimum for public health actions and services: at least 15% of its net current revenue (RCL) for the year.

Constitutional Amendment 95 of 2016 brought forward the 15%-of-net-current-revenue floor to 2017 and, for later years, replaced it with the previous year's floor adjusted for consumer price inflation (IPCA), as part of a cap on federal primary spending planned to run from 2017 to 2036.

Constitutional Amendment 126 of 2022 provided for the repeal of that transitional rule once a new fiscal-framework law was signed; with Complementary Law 200 of 30 August 2023 it was revoked, and the permanent constitutional rules for the health and education floors applied again.

Complementary Law 141 of 2012 requires the states and the Federal District to spend at least 12% of their revenue from state taxes and from specified federal transfers on public health actions and services each year, after deducting the shares passed on to their municipalities.

The same law requires municipalities (and the Federal District) to spend at least 15% of their revenue from municipal taxes and from specified federal and state transfers on public health actions and services each year.

According to the Ministry of Health's public health budget system (SIOPS), in 2021 the states and the Federal District spent R$ 11.4 billion of their own revenue on public health actions and services above the constitutional minimum, and the municipalities R$ 40.0 billion.

Under the 1988 Constitution as first written, social contributions financed health, pensions and social assistance in the social security budget without distinction; the 1998 pension reform reserved contributions levied on payroll exclusively for paying general-regime (RGPS) pension benefits.

In IBGE's health satellite account, final consumption of health goods and services was 9.7% of GDP in 2021: 4.0% of GDP by government and 5.7% by households and non-profit institutions serving households. These are national-accounts final-consumption figures, not the System of Health Accounts definition used by WHO and the OECD.

locator.section: Despesas com consumo final de bens e serviços de saúde como percentual do PIB, por setor institucional

financing.statement: In the satellite account, households' spending on private health services (which counts all payments to health plans, including those made by employers) was their largest health expense: 67.5% of household final health consumption in 2019, 64.9% in 2020 and 63.7% in 2021.
Medicines were 32.5% of households' health spending in 2020 (R$ 143.1 billion) and 33.7% in 2021 (R$ 168.3 billion).
In April 2025 private medical and hospital plans had 52,331,258 beneficiary enrolments, 1.94% more than a year earlier.
According to the ANS, private health plans received R$ 312.1 billion in premium payments (contraprestações) and paid R$ 256.8 billion in health care expenses in 2024.

locator.section: Figura 1: Grandes Números do Setor de Saúde Suplementar

financing.statement: Enrolment in medical plans grew most in employer-sponsored group plans (3.90%), which cover people linked to a company by employment; individual plans lost 1.38% of their beneficiaries between 2023 and 2024 and group plans joined through professional or trade associations lost 4.87%.
The Federal Revenue Service estimated federal tax expenditures (revenue forgone through tax benefits) for 2026 at R$ 612.84 billion, equal to 4.43% of GDP and 20.20% of the revenue it administers.
By budget function, health accounts for 17.41% of the estimated 2026 federal tax expenditures, second only to commerce and services (22.54%).
The Federal Revenue Service lists the personal income tax deduction for medical expenses (Law 9.250/1995, art. 8, II, a) as a tax expenditure with no end date.
It also lists as an open-ended corporate income tax (IRPJ) expenditure the medical, dental and pharmaceutical assistance that companies provide to their employees (Law 9.249/1995, art. 13, V).
Unlike education expenses, personal income tax deductions for health expenses have no ceiling, although the deduction cannot exceed the taxpayer's income.
An Ipea study put the corporate income tax revenue forgone on health in 2018 at R$ 8.3 billion; companies can deduct the health care they pay for their employees from taxable profit.
The Ipea author argues that health tax subsidies burden the public budget and are regressive at a time of underfunding of the SUS.

The Federal Court of Accounts (TCU) reports that the deductions of health and education expenses from personal income tax cost R$ 34.76 billion in 2025, the fifth-largest federal tax expenditure; the figure combines health and education.
The TCU rates these personal income tax deductions high-risk: it finds them strongly regressive, with 88% of the benefit going to the richest 20%, and inconsistent with the universal SUS.

For the tax relief on medical assistance that employers provide to workers, the TCU reports that evaluations recommended reviewing the benefit (controlling, reducing or ending it) and redirecting the money to the SUS, and that this relief goes mostly to the richest part of the population.

covered.statement: Brazil now has a nationwide network of primary, emergency and mental health services, plus specialised centres for transplantation, HIV/AIDS and cancer, supported by a comprehensive pharmaceutical policy.
Expansion of the SUS widened public health programmes such as immunisation, tuberculosis and HIV, and complex services such as organ transplants, cancer care and kidney dialysis.
The national essential medicines list grew from 327 medicines in 2002 to 869 in 2017, alongside policies to improve access to medicines and promote generics.

A national technology-incorporation commission (Comissão Nacional de Incorporação de Tecnologias) was created in 2011 to back evidence-based decisions on adopting new medicines and technologies in the SUS.

A 2026 study of Brazil's health technology assessment system found broad recognition of CONITEC's central role in coordinating evidence generation and appraisal, but identified possible conflicts of interest and sole reliance on government funding as challenges.
Of 199 drugs incorporated into the SUS that the study analysed, 64 were projected to be cost-saving, with projected savings of Int$6.67 billion.

Family health teams were originally made up of a general practitioner, a nurse, a nursing technician or assistant and four to six community health workers chosen from the local community, who make routine home visits to around 150 families in small areas.

locator.section: The transformation of the Family Health Program into a strategy

cost_sharing.statement: Since 2004 the Popular Pharmacy Programme (Farmácia Popular) has widened access to medicines at subsidised prices with low copayments.
Out-of-pocket payments, though reduced, made up nearly half of private health spending in this 2018 analysis and remained a considerable burden for households.
Medicines were the main component of out-of-pocket health spending, making up 85% of such payments in the lowest consumption deciles.
Catastrophic health spending has declined since 2004, but medicines remain an important item in the budgets of the poorest families.

financial_hardship.statement: More than 10 million Brazilians a year are pushed into poverty by out-of-pocket health payments: 4.87% of people, against 2.5% globally and 1.8% in Latin America and the Caribbean.
One household in three devotes over 10% of its budget to health; financial hardship is significantly more frequent among poor Brazilians, reaching 37% in the bottom consumption deciles.

additional_care.statement: In 2019, 59.7 million people (28.5% of residents) had a private medical or dental health plan, not significantly different from 27.9% in 2013.

locator.section: Cobertura de plano de saúde, médico ou odontológico

additional_care.statement: In 2019 plan coverage was highest in the Southeast (37.5%), South (32.8%) and Centre-West (28.9%) and lowest in the North (14.7%) and Northeast (16.6%).

locator.section: Cobertura de plano de saúde, médico ou odontológico

additional_care.statement: Only 2.2% of people with no income or up to a quarter of the minimum wage had a medical plan, against 86.8% of those receiving more than five minimum wages a month.

locator.section: Cobertura de plano de saúde, médico ou odontológico

additional_care.statement: Dental plan coverage was much less common than medical plan coverage (12.9% against 26.0%).

locator.section: Cobertura de plano de saúde, médico ou odontológico

additional_care.statement: Private medical insurance grew from 30.5 million people (17.6%) in 2000 to 50.3 million (24.8%) in 2014, then fell to 47.3 million (22.8%) in 2017 as incomes and employment declined.

Under a 1998 law, private health plans must reimburse the SUS whenever one of their members is treated in it; Agora Tem Especialistas lets plan companies join the programme and offset these reimbursement debts.

locator.section: Planos de saúde e ressarcimento ao SUS

access.statement: The basic health unit (Unidade Básica de Saúde) was the facility the largest share of people (46.8%) said they usually went to for care, followed by private practices or clinics (22.9%) and public emergency units or public hospital emergency departments (14.1%).

locator.section: Acesso e utilização dos serviços de saúde

access.statement: In 2019, 76.2% of people (159.6 million) had seen a doctor in the previous 12 months, up from 71.2% in 2013.

locator.section: Acesso e utilização dos serviços de saúde

access.statement: In 2019, 60.0% of households (44.0 million) were registered with a family health unit, up from 53.3% in 2013.
Of people hospitalised for 24 hours or more, 64.6% (8.9 million) were admitted through the SUS in 2019.

Reliance on the SUS for hospital care falls steeply with income: in 2019 the last hospital stay was through the SUS for 95.0% of hospitalised people with household income per person of up to a quarter of the minimum wage, but for only 6.8% of those with more than five minimum wages.

Brazil has almost doubled its medical workforce since 2003, to 2.77 doctors per 1,000 people, with the largest increase after the 2013 legislation; poorer, remote states gained, but most new doctors and students are still in richer regions.
Doctor shortages persist in rural areas and in primary care, and specialists are concentrated in the private sector and unevenly spread across the country.

outcomes.statement: Infant mortality fell from 53.4 to 12.7 deaths per 1,000 live births between 1990 and 2023, life expectancy rose from 65 years in 1985 to 76.8 years in 2025, and polio (1989) and measles (2000) were eliminated.
In the GBD 2019 study, Brazil's Healthcare Access and Quality (HAQ) Index score for ages 0-74 was 53.0 (95% uncertainty interval 51.5-54.3) in 2019, 17.5 points higher than in 1990.

locator.table: Table: HAQ Index estimates by location, 2019 overall (0-74 years) and absolute change 1990-2019 overall

outcomes.statement: By age group in the GBD 2019 study, Brazil's 2019 HAQ Index score was 62.4 for ages 0-14, 53.4 for ages 15-64 and 48.6 for ages 65-74.

locator.table: Table: HAQ Index estimates by location, 2019, young (0-14), working (15-64) and post-working (65-74) age groups

outcomes.statement: In the GBD 2016 HAQ Index, Brazil was in the sixth of ten deciles nationally; the Federal District reached the eighth decile (score 75.4), while most states, especially northern ones, were in the fifth.

Disparities in HAQ Index scores between Brazil's states widened slightly after 2000, with the absolute gap going from 17.2 points in 1990 to 20.4 in 2016; Brazil's overall progress was more consistent over time than Mexico's.
A study of all Brazilian microregions in 2008-2017 found no significant effect of the extra primary care doctors supplied by the Mais Médicos programme on hospitalisation or mortality rates.

After Cuban doctors left the More Doctors programme, affected municipalities saw lasting falls in chronic-disease care, while use of urgent services such as maternal care and infection treatment soon recovered; the fall in use did not translate into changes in health outcomes.

costs.statement: A 2026 review of the Family Health Strategy called chronic underfunding of the SUS a central obstacle to expanding primary care, noting public health spending below 4% of GDP against roughly 7% in countries with universal systems.

locator.section: Desafios: Financiamento (Portuguese-language version of the article)

costs.statement: Municipal health spending per person grew 226% in real terms between 2003 and 2014 (from R$315.7 to R$716.5), then fell 6.3% to R$617.1 in 2016.
Most of the federal budget goes to debt service, which limits fiscal space for other areas; debt service rose from 50.3% of the federal budget in 2013 to 57.0% in 2016.

Among drugs paid for solely by the Ministry of Health, the cumulative projected incremental budget impact equalled 29% of the CEAF (specialised pharmaceutical care) budget in 2024, after exceeding 45% from 2019 to 2022.
In 2019, lawsuits consumed 25.2% of the resources of the Specialised Component of Pharmaceutical Care, with 21% going to 10 medicines.

what_works.statement: A 2019 review concluded that Brazil, despite successes and setbacks, has achieved nearly universal access to health-care services for its population.
The Family Health Strategy's population coverage rose from 13.2 million people (7.8%) in 2000 to 120.2 million (58.5%) in 2016.

Family health coverage is distributed equitably: in the 2019 national health survey it reached 74% of the poorest income fifth against 38% of the richest, and registered people more often had a regular source of care (79% vs 73%).

locator.section: Impact of the expansion of FHS coverage on access and population health

what_works.statement: Studies link the Family Health Strategy to lower infant and under-5 mortality and fewer ambulatory-care-sensitive admissions among adults and older people, especially where coverage was consistently high; effects were larger in vulnerable groups.

locator.section: Impact of the expansion of FHS coverage on access and population health

what_works.statement: Medical students became more diverse after the 2013 More Doctors legislation: women rose from 55.5% of students in 2013 to 61.4% in 2023 and mixed-race students from 19.4% to 25.5%, though most students remain white and from fee-paying secondary schools.

A review found CONITEC's decisions consistent with affordability principles in health technology assessment, judged on the evidence available at each decision rather than on real-world data after incorporation into the SUS.
After Cuban doctors left the More Doctors Program, supply-side responses and patients diverting to other sources of care helped mitigate major harm to population health at the market level.

problems.statement: A 2018 analysis found persistent structural problems in the SUS, including weak organisation and governance, low public funding and poor resource allocation, leaving large regional gaps in access and outcomes that hit poorer regions and groups hardest.

Chronic underfunding, made worse by the 2016 spending cap, limits the system, and specialised services, intensive care beds and diagnostic equipment are concentrated in wealthier regions and in the private sector.
Waiting lists for surgery, biopsies and radiotherapy are long and still growing, and the cancer care network has not kept pace with the rising cancer burden.
Maternal mortality remains high for Brazil's level of development, and the health workforce is unevenly distributed because strategies to attract, retain and train staff across regions fall short.
Shortages of some specialist services and weak administrative capacity have produced poor-quality hospital services with long waits.

Courts help secure access when the state fails to supply medicines already in the SUS, but orders to buy medicines not incorporated into the system compromise access to medicines for the wider population.

Among households registered with a family health unit for a year or more, 38.4% (15.4 million) received a monthly visit from a community health worker or family health team member in 2019, down from 47.2% in 2013.

Among households registered with a family health unit for a year or more, about 23.8% (9.5 million) had never been visited by a community health worker or team member in 2019, a sharp rise from 17.7% (5.3 million) in 2013.

Under Previne Brasil, the primary care financing model, only one of seven performance indicators (syphilis and HIV testing in pregnancy: 62.5% against a 60% target) met its target on average across the four-month periods from early 2022 to early 2023.
Student achievement scores and resources point to significantly lower teaching quality in private medical schools.

The authors conclude that, despite progress in implementing universal coverage, financial protection is not yet guaranteed, especially for the poor, and that wider access to affordable essential medicines is key to improving it.

reforms.statement: Agora Tem Especialistas was launched in May 2025 through Provisional Measure 1,301, merging the National Programme for Reducing Queues with the More Access to Specialists programme (PMAE).

Article 1 of the law creates the Agora Tem Especialistas programme, joined by private hospitals (for-profit or not), to expand beds and services and cut waiting times for specialist consultations, procedures and tests.
The law caps the financial credits granted under the programme at R$2 billion a year.

A 2026 analysis argued that Agora Tem Especialistas should not be seen as privatising the universal system, since it does not raise private health spending, expand private plans or hand public responsibilities to the private sector, but said its effect on regional and public-private inequalities must be monitored.

PMAQ-AB was progressively dismantled from 2017 amid political and institutional change and ended in 2019; its successor, Previne Brasil, narrowed assessment to a small number of process indicators and was itself discontinued in 2024.
A 2018-2024 trend study using Pernambuco as a case found the federal government's share of primary care financing was greater after Previne was discontinued.

From 2019 to 2023, Previne Brasil replaced funding based on the whole catchment population with funding by individually registered patients, which the authors say limited collective action, restricted access to registered patients and undermined universality, comprehensiveness and equity.

In 2023, with the rebuilding of the SUS and renewed priority for family health, the NASF programme was reformulated into federally co-financed multidisciplinary primary care teams with a broader scope, including telehealth.

The PMMB was relaunched in 2023, emphasising rebuilding teams, training and retaining doctors in priority areas, after the 2019 Doctors for Brazil Program (PMpB) proved slow and limited in reach, and amid political change.
Under MP n. 1,165/2023, More Doctors offered 15,000 new vacancies.

Constitutional Amendment 126/2022 opened R$145 billion of budget space for 2023 and abolished the Temer government's expenditure ceiling, which had in practice frozen real federal primary spending for 20 years.

The third Lula government's new fiscal framework (the New Sustainable Fiscal Regime, PLP 93/2023, still before the Senate when this editorial was written) would limit real growth in federal spending to 70% of real growth in primary revenue, with a maximum of 2.5% real growth.

At the end of 2018, after the elections, Cuba suspended its PAHO-mediated agreement with Brazil and withdrew most Cuban doctors; under health minister Mandetta, the Bolsonaro government launched Médicos pelo Brasil, which required national validation of diplomas obtained abroad.

Constitutional Amendment 95, passed in December 2016, limited federal primary spending on health for 20 years: 15% of net current revenue in 2017 and then 2017 levels adjusted for inflation, with a projected decline of R$415 billion in the health budget by 2036 as described in 2018 (the ceiling has since been abolished; see the Amendment 126/2022 entry).
In 2013 the Rousseff government launched the More Doctors (Mais Médicos) programme, sending more than 18,000 doctors, mostly from Cuba, to underserved areas to expand primary care.
